questions.stem_markdown: A 14-year-old is seen alone during a general paediatric review. She says she has never been sexually active but feels increasingly distressed about being attracted to girls and asks whether sexual health even applies to her. Which response is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Sexual health is broader than intercourse or pregnancy prevention; it includes physical, emotional, mental and social wellbeing related to sexuality, so it is reasonable to talk about how this is affecting you.
Sexual health questions are mainly for young people who are already having intercourse.
If there is no current STI or pregnancy risk, sexuality concerns sit outside adolescent health care.
It is best to defer discussion of sexuality until late adolescence, when identity is more settled.
The main purpose of sexual health review is to decide whether contraception is needed.

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes define sexual health as a state of physical, emotional, mental and social wellbeing related to sexuality, not just intercourse, contraception, or STI prevention. They also frame becoming comfortable with one's own sexuality and intimate relationships as part of adolescent development. That makes option A the best response.

why_others_wrong.B: This narrows sexual health to intercourse, which is inconsistent with the broader wellbeing definition in the notes.
why_others_wrong.C: Sexuality concerns are still relevant even without immediate STI or pregnancy risk.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes do not support delaying discussion of sexuality until late adolescence.
why_others_wrong.E: Contraception is only one part of sexual health, not its sole purpose.

key_takeaways: Sexual health is broader than intercourse or contraception.
Adolescent sexual health includes emotional, mental and social wellbeing.
Comfort with sexuality and intimate relationships is a developmental task of adolescence.

questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old asks to speak privately and says she has been having consensual sex with her 18-year-old boyfriend. She asks you to reassure her that it is fine because she agreed. Based on the notes, what is the **best response**?

options.text: In NSW, 16 is the age of consent, so consent alone does not make this straightforward; it needs a careful discussion of what has been happening and her safety.
Because she agreed, NSW law is only relevant if force or obvious coercion was used.
In NSW, consensual sexual activity is automatically lawful from age 15.
It only becomes a legal issue if pregnancy occurs.
Age of consent only applies to vaginal intercourse, not to other sexual acts.

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes state that in NSW the age of consent is 16, and they discuss sexual intercourse and other sexual acts in that framework. A 15-year-old should therefore not be given blanket reassurance that agreement alone settles the issue. The best response is careful, non-dismissive discussion rather than simplistic reassurance.

why_others_wrong.B: This ignores the age-of-consent issue by treating force as the only relevant legal concern.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes state that the age of consent is 16, not 15.
why_others_wrong.D: Pregnancy is not what determines whether age-of-consent concerns exist.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes explicitly include sexual intercourse and other sexual acts.

key_takeaways: In NSW, the age of consent is 16.
Consent alone does not justify blanket reassurance in an under-16 scenario.
Age-of-consent discussions should be handled carefully and non-dismissively.

questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old says she had sexual intercourse once 4 months ago and is not currently in a relationship. She thinks there is nothing else to cover because it was just one time. Which response is **best supported** by the notes?

options.text: It is still worth covering pregnancy and STI prevention and whether any follow-up is needed, because a first sexual experience should not be assumed to mean a stable monogamous pattern.
Further sexual health discussion can wait unless she starts having sex regularly.
A single sexual experience in mid-adolescence usually suggests she has already moved into monogamy.
If she is not currently partnered, only emotional follow-up matters.
Prevention planning is mainly useful once there are multiple partners or obvious condom problems.

questions.explanation_markdown: Louisa notes that there is an increasing gap between first sexual experience and monogamy. That means a one-off sexual experience should not be used to assume a stable low-risk pattern. The best response is to keep prevention and follow-up discussion open, rather than closing it down because the event was single or not recent.

why_others_wrong.B: This delays prevention and follow-up based on frequency rather than need.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes specifically argue against assuming first sexual experience coincides with monogamy.
why_others_wrong.D: Emotional follow-up may matter, but the notes do not support excluding prevention discussion.
why_others_wrong.E: The threshold for useful prevention counselling is not limited to multiple partners or known condom problems.

key_takeaways: Do not assume first sexual experience equals stable monogamy.
Prevention counselling can still be relevant after a single sexual experience.
Sexual-health follow-up should not rely only on partner count.

questions.stem_markdown: A 17-year-old says she only ever has sex when she has been drinking at parties and thinks that means her risk is really just an alcohol issue, not a sexual-health issue. What is the **best next approach**?

options.text: Treat this as both a substance-use and sexual-health issue, because alcohol use in adolescence is linked to risky sexual behaviour and a notable minority of sexually active teens report sex when drunk or high.
Focus on alcohol only, because infrequent sex does not meaningfully change sexual-health risk.
Focus on sexual health only, because the alcohol history is separate.
Defer sexual-health discussion until she has stopped drinking.
Limit sexual-health follow-up to cases with multiple partners.

questions.explanation_markdown: The CAH notes state that teenage drinking is associated with risky sexual behaviours, and that 20% of sexually active teens reported being drunk or high in their last sexual experience. Louisa also frames alcohol and other drug use as part of adolescent risk-taking with broader bio-psycho-social harms. The best response is therefore an integrated discussion rather than treating alcohol and sexual health as unrelated domains.

why_others_wrong.B: This incorrectly assumes infrequent sex can be separated from sexual-health risk.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes support linking substance use and risky sexual behaviour, not treating them as unrelated.
why_others_wrong.D: Deferring sexual-health discussion misses a current prevention opportunity.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes do not restrict sexual-health follow-up to multiple-partner scenarios.

key_takeaways: Alcohol use and sexual-health risk often need to be addressed together.
Sex when drunk or high is a recognised adolescent sexual-health concern in the notes.
Risky sexual behaviour is not defined only by partner number.
